title: Who Needs Labels? Adapting Vision Foundation Models With the Metadata You Already Have
claim: Metadata that already accompanies scientific images can adapt a generic foundation model without labels, beating supervised fine-tuning and published specialised systems.
layout: 3 panels: image grid left, two-step pipeline top-right, bar chart bottom-right
description: The left panel (a) is a 2x2 grid of real images from four scientific domains: HPA fluorescence microscopy, FMoW satellite imagery, iWildCam camera-trap wildlife, and a MIMIC-CXR chest X-ray. Under each image are magenta metadata names, such as plates, antibody, cell line, country, weather, trap, timestamp, age and view position. Icons mark each one as discrete (dots) or continuous (double arrow). The top right, panel (b) FINO, is a two-step box-and-arrow diagram. Step 1, representation adaptation, feeds images into a backbone with a flame icon. The backbone and metadata feed SSL and WSL loss ovals. Step 2, lightweight probing, uses a frozen backbone (snowflake icon) and a trainable probe, with labels feeding a supervised loss. The bottom right, panel (c), is a bar chart of performance relative to published references. It has bars for frozen DINOv3, supervised fine-tuning and FINO on four datasets. The FINO bars in magenta reach or exceed the green 100% reference line.
caption: Learning with metadata. Scientific datasets (a) often include metadata describing their content and acquisition. FINO uses these signals as weak supervision (WSL), together with a self-supervised objective (SSL), to adapt a generic foundation model without task labels (b). In matched evaluations, its frozen representations outperform supervised fine-tuning; the right panel compares FINO means to reported specialised-system results under differing protocols (c).
abstract: We propose a label-free approach to adapt powerful but generic vision foundation models to specialized scientific domains. Standard supervised fine-tuning is often ill-suited to these settings: labels are scarce, and task-specific training can reduce the generality needed to cope with complex domain shifts. We instead leverage metadata to adapt representations to new domains in a weakly-supervised manner. Our method, FINO, combines a standard self-supervised objective with flexible metadata guidance that handles both highly granular discrete metadata and continuous metadata. It encourages the representation to preserve informative factors while suppressing spurious ones. Across subcellular fluorescence microscopy, Earth observation, wildlife monitoring, and medical imaging, FINO outperforms matched self-supervised and fully supervised adaptation baselines. Complete-adaptation repeats confirm consistent performance across domains. Without task labels for backbone adaptation, FINO also obtains higher reported scores than selected specialised systems on three domains and matches the fourth under differing cross-paper protocols. Code is available at github.com/facebookresearch/dinov3/tree/FINO.
